probe.format_note: 16:9 landscape, one full-frame film. Stereo AAC 48 kHz. Half-second RMS measured, not listened to: a steady music bed that alternates about -21.6 / -23.7 dB on a 1.0 s period across the film; one deep dip at 2.5 s (-35.6 dB) followed by the loudest early peak at 3.0 s (-18.4 dB), which lands on the first UI scene; louder, irregular passages at 12-14.5 s, 15.5-18 s and 68-71 s match the on-screen spoken captions; the bed sits lower (about -28 dB) under the live shot at 66.5-68 s; short dips near 11, 15, 41, 65, 71 and 73.5 s (about -28 dB).

method: ffprobe; ffmpeg contact sheets fps=2 at 480 px (13 sheets, all viewed); scene detect gt(scene,0.3): 2.57, 2.60, 2.73, 2.90, 7.17, 8.27, 10.73, 11.97, 15.17, 18.17, 20.13, 21.17, 24.97, 27.60, 29.97, 33.63, 39.23, 47.27, 49.23, 59.90, 61.67, 65.00, 70.47, 73.00 s; dense sheets at 10-15 fps over 2.2-3.8, 6.4-8.0, 12.0-13.6, 17.4-19.0, 21.0-23.4, 34.4-36.8, 43.6-46.0, 61.2-63.6 and 71.2-72.8 s; half-second RMS of the audio with astats. Boundaries at 2.47, 3.0, 5.0, 35.75, 43.7, 45.8 and 54.9 s are not scene-detect cuts: they are whips or flashes placed by eye, accurate to about 0.25 s at 5.0 and 54.9 s and about 0.1 s at the others. Colours were read by eye, not sampled. The audio was measured, not heard, so voice versus music is inferred from loudness and captions.

visual_language: A software workflow demo told as a small comedy: a real person asks a helper for something out loud, the helper does the job on screen while the person gets on with their day, and the film ends on a joke about the cost. Two media alternate: code-built UI on flat coloured stages, and short, calm, photographic live-action cut-aways that act as breathing room. Typography: one clean neo-grotesque sans in regular weight, no heavy display headlines; captions and reasoning lines are sentences, set white and small to large purely by camera scale. Text appears by word fade in reserved places (captions, prompt) or by a soft sweep with an accent-coloured leading edge (reasoning lines), never by a bouncy animation. Rhythm: 28 shots in 75.5 s, average about 2.7 s, and much shorter within scenes: UI shots contain several jumps in scale, so the eye gets a new framing every 0.5-1.5 s, while live shots run 1.2-5.5 s. Cut-to-beat is not proven: 13 of 20 cuts (leaving out the flash at 2.57-2.90 s) fall within 0.25 s of a whole second where chance alone gives about half; the one clear sync is the first hit at 3.0 s. Moves are snappy in with strong ease-out, usually from heavy motion blur, then a long gentle drift on every hold; the frame is rarely fully still. Scale is the main editing tool: UI is shown at huge scale on one element, then pulled back to the whole window (or the reverse), and very often the same panel is shown at three sizes. Palette: hot two-tone pink backdrop, near-black UI, one acid accent, one royal blue that belongs only to the helper, and off-white for the opening pages; live action is desaturated cream and warm grey, which makes the pink feel louder. Signature moments: the palette-swap burst into white on the first hit; the plain pointer morphing into the glowing blue helper; the speech pill growing out of a dot; the accent stroke tracing a found result; the halftone ring uncovering a result; the one-word 'done' pill; the whip into one number that counts down; the pull-back to a sight gag.
look: UI scenes are flat with 2.5D touches: flat dark window panels with rounded corners and thin hairline borders, floating on a flat backdrop with a very large, soft drop shadow, sometimes tilted a few degrees in perspective; there are no real 3D objects. Light comes only from glows: soft blue halo on the helper, lime bloom on accents, red glow on errors. Materials are matte dark panels, glossy blue pills with a light top edge, and translucent grey ghost tiles. Depth of field is used heavily as an effect: whole UI plates held in strong lens blur behind a sharp pointer, and defocus pulls between text states; motion blur on every whip, plus radial zoom blur. Backgrounds are an off-white empty stage, a near-black violet-grey empty stage, or a hot pink field with one diagonal or slow-morphing wave ribbons in a second pink, with no ground plane. Live shots are realistic and photographic, soft window light, shallow depth of field, muted colour grade, and they cannot be matched in code as such.
code_translation: About two thirds of the film's time is code-native and fits the HTML/CSS/SVG pipeline in headless Chromium: floating UI windows as real DOM, CSS 3D perspective for small tilts, CSS filter blur for lens-blur plates and defocus pulls, directional and radial blur by frame blending or scaled copies for whips and zoom-throughs, SVG path morph for pointer → helper arrow, width-animated pill for the speech bubble, animated stroke-dashoffset with glow for the traced result, a canvas or SVG halftone mask with a growing radius for the reveal, a gradient text mask for the accent leading edge, SVG morphing ribbons for the pink backdrop. It is not a 3D film and three.js is not required. The live-action shots, about a third of the running time counted with the footage card, are the part that cannot be built: L4 replaces each with a scene taken from our voice-over, drawn in the film's own rendering (flat UI-world illustration or simple 3D) and keeping only its job in the rhythm: a short calm breath between busy UI scenes, a side task that progresses, a comic set-up and turn. Never a real face. Stand-in images inside the UI (thumbnails, preview, result) are replaced by owner assets or by code-drawn pictures.
continuity: The pointer as a character: one on-screen pointer changes state and colour (plain → glowing helper → plain), travels across every UI scene and links them; its colour belongs to no other element.
Speech in place of voice: the helper talks through a small pill that grows out of a dot beside it and collapses back to a line when it has finished.
Same words, two places: words first seen in a spoken caption reappear typed into the UI, so the viewer connects the request to the action.
Ask, then wait, then return: the film cuts away to the person's calm side task and comes back to find the work has moved on, without showing the waiting.
A side task with its own small story progresses in stages across the cut-aways, in parallel with the main job.
Scale jumps within one object: the same panel appears extreme close, wide and medium in fast succession, so a cut reads as a camera move.
Backdrop as a carrier: a panel leaves the frame while the backdrop stays, and the next object arrives on it, so no cut is felt.
Text as the anchor across a whip: a line stays on screen during a vertical whip and sits above the next card, which ties the reasoning to its result.

Reveal through texture: a result is uncovered by a ring of accent dots opening from the centre; the same dot texture appears in the opening title, so the film's first and later reveals share one device.
Group handling: many items are selected together, travel as translucent ghost tiles and land in their new place, so a change of screen reads as one continuous act.
Motion hides the cut: a person's or panel's own fast move (standing up, a rotation, a whip) takes the eye and the cut lands inside it.
Bookend through the pointer: the helper is born at the start of the job and returns to a plain pointer when the job is over; the last hit (a number, then a pull-back) answers the opening request.
risks: Third-party film of unknown origin: ADAPT only. Never copy the logos, product names, English copy, UI screens, file and folder names, the account name, the percentages, the car, the person or the kitchen, or the shot order one by one.

About 34% of the running time is live-action or filmed footage that cannot be built in code; the photographic look and the human reaction are lost. Those beats must be redesigned from our voice-over in the film's own rendering, never as a fake real person.

The comic ending (shock, then the number, then the spill on the floor) depends on a real performance and on a figure: use it only if our voiceover supports a joke, and any number must come from our approved package.

Source is 16:9 landscape; a 9:16 film must rebuild each composition vertically. The floating wide window becomes a phone-like panel or a close section of a window, and long sideways pans become vertical moves or shorter lines, inside the 9:16 safe zone.

UI holds are short and many labels are tiny by design: Persian text hold times and minimum sizes win over this pace (readability ranks above the reference); tiny labels are texture only and never carry meaning the viewer must read.

The reference reads left to right: sweeps, pans, typing and the left-hand entrances follow references/rtl-grammar.md for Persian. The accent leading-edge sweep and any letter-by-letter typing must not break Persian joining: reveal whole words, or use a mask over fully shaped text.

Colours were read by eye. The hot pink, near-black, lime and royal blue map onto brand colour roles (main field, dark surface, accent, helper colour); never used as literal hex values, and a brand's banned colours win.
The palette-swap burst in r1-s2 steps through full-frame colour changes every 2-3 frames; keep it short and within brand roles, and treat it as a possible flicker risk for sensitive viewers.
The reference has its own music and spoken audio and they were measured, not heard. Our film's cuts follow the voiceover first, and L6 places accents on our cuts rather than reusing its sound.
